Running at scale

Service

pcs-service is a process that reads one TOML file, loads a pipeline, and runs it until you stop it. Everything it will refuse to start on, it refuses at load time.

In one line
A TOML file plus a .wasm component becomes a long-running process with health checks
You need
pcs-service built with --features service,wasm; use service-cluster,wasm for Raft
Read this if
You have a pipeline that works and now need it to run unattended, behind a readiness probe, on a schedule
On this page
  1. Install and build

Install and build

The binary lives in the pcs-service crate and is gated on the service feature. Neither service nor service-cluster implies wasm, and without wasm the config parser has no [pipeline.wasm] table to bind — so both feature sets below name it explicitly.

-p pcs-service is not required from the workspace root; cargo resolves --features against the members that define them. It is written out below anyway, because it makes the command copy-pasteable from any directory in the tree.

Bashpick the feature set you actually need
# Single node, WASM pipelines. This is the usual build.
cargo build --release -p pcs-service --bin pcs-service --features service,wasm

# Same, plus Raft cluster mode.
cargo build --release -p pcs-service --bin pcs-service --features service-cluster,wasm

# Or put it on PATH.
cargo install --path crates/pcs-service --features service-cluster,wasm

service pulls in io, distributed and tracing along with axum, clap and the Prometheus exporter. service-cluster is service plus distributed-raft. Neither of them implies wasm.

Sharp edge

Neither feature set implies wasm, and without it PipelineSpec has no fields at all while still rejecting unknown keys. So a [pipeline.wasm] table in a --features service build is not ignored, it is a parse failure: unknown field `wasm`, there are no fields. Every example config in the repository declares that table, so build with service,wasm or service-cluster,wasm.

The two run modes

The top-level mode key picks the runner. Both drive the same PipelineRuntime trait object, so a pipeline does not know or care which one is running it.

mode = "standalone"mode = "cluster"
Feature service service-cluster
Coordination None. One process, one dataset. Raft over TCP between the declared [[peers]].
Ingest [[sources]] drained into the dataset each iteration. PartitionSource — batches are claimed, not read. [[sources]] is rejected.
Pacing [run_mode]: continuous, one_shot, or interval. As fast as claims arrive, until cancelled.
On restart Re-reads its sources from the beginning. Resumes from the checkpoint recorded under its lease.
Uses node.data_dir No — required to be non-empty, never written. Yes: raft-log.redb, cluster-app.redb, bootstrap.lock, node-id.

A standalone iteration is seven steps: check for cancellation, drain each source into the dataset, call runtime.run_on(&mut dataset), drain the dataset into each sink, publish the stats snapshot, dataset.clear(), then sleep according to [run_mode]. continuous pauses 100 ms between iterations; one_shot exits after the first.

When the runtime is a WASM guest, that third step does not execute on the async worker. WasmPipelineRuntime builds the store, instantiates the component and calls run-batch inside tokio::task::spawn_blocking, because the guest is linked against the synchronous WASI implementation: any WASI import the guest touches routes through Handle::block_on, which panics outright on a thread that is already driving a tokio runtime. Only Arrow IPC bytes cross onto that thread and back.

Errors do not stop the loop. A source failure logs a warning; a runtime failure logs an error and the sinks are still flushed; a sink failure logs an error. All three increment iteration_errors, which /status reports.

Constraint

Cluster mode rejects [[sources]] at config-validation time, before anything starts. The cluster runner ingests through PartitionSource, a pull mechanism, so a declared Source would be silently ignored and the pipeline would sit idle. Register batches from a producer instead. [[sinks]] is allowed, but each node writes its own share.

The TOML file

One document, parsed strictly. ${VAR} placeholders are substituted from the environment before parsing — an unset ${VAR} is an error, and ${VAR:-default} falls back.

TOMLservice.toml — every key here exists
# Picks the runner. "standalone" or "cluster".
mode = "standalone"

[node]
id = 1                            # u64, unique and stable across restarts
name = "pcs-1"                    # optional label for logs and /status
data_dir = "/var/lib/pcs/node-1"  # must be non-empty; the cluster runner writes here

# Standalone pacing. kind = "continuous" | "one_shot" | "interval".
# interval_ms applies to "interval" only. Defaults to continuous if omitted.
[run_mode]
kind = "interval"
interval_ms = 5000

# The pipeline. A wasm32-wasip2 component implementing pcs:pipeline/pcs-pipeline.
[pipeline.wasm]
module = "pipelines/orders.wasm"
# Optional integrity check, verified before JIT compilation.
# A leading "sha3-256:" prefix is accepted.
# sha3_256 = "6f1c...c4"

# String key/values the guest pulls with the host-io get-config import.
# Values are strings; the guest parses numerics itself.
[pipeline.wasm.config]
fx_eur = "1.08"
batch_size = "500"

[[sources]]
name = "orders_in"                # unique
type = "ParquetSource"            # factory lookup key
target_component = "Order"        # must be a component the guest declares

[sources.config]                  # opaque; handed to the factory verbatim
path = "/data/in/orders.parquet"

[[sinks]]
name = "orders_out"
type = "ParquetSink"
source_component = "Order"

[sinks.config]
path = "/data/out/orders.parquet"

[[sinks.config.schema_fields]]
name = "id"
type = "Int64"
nullable = false

[[sinks.config.schema_fields]]
name = "usd_amount"
type = "Float64"
nullable = false

[http]
bind = "0.0.0.0:8080"   # default; must parse as a SocketAddr
disabled = false        # true turns the control plane off entirely

[observability]
log_format = "pretty"   # "pretty" or "json"
log_level = "info"

In cluster mode the flattened block at the top of the document changes: drop [run_mode], add the Raft timings and the peer list.

TOMLthe cluster-mode header, in place of [run_mode]
mode = "cluster"
bootstrap = true              # true on exactly one node, on first bring-up only
lease_ttl_ms = 30000          # must be >= 3 x election_timeout_ms
election_timeout_ms = 1500
heartbeat_interval_ms = 300
snapshot_log_interval = 10000 # snapshot every N committed log entries

# Every member, including this node. node.id must appear here.
# addr is the Raft transport address, not the HTTP control-plane port.
[[peers]]
id = 1
addr = "10.0.0.1:9000"

[[peers]]
id = 2
addr = "10.0.0.2:9000"

[[peers]]
id = 3
addr = "10.0.0.3:9000"

The type strings on sources and sinks are looked up in a registry. These eight ship in the box, all behind the io feature that service already enables:

SourcesSinksRequired config keys
ParquetSourceParquetSinksource: path. sink: path, schema_fields
CsvSourceCsvSinkpath, schema_fields, optional has_headers
JsonSourceJsonSinkpath, schema_fields
ChannelSourceChannelSinknone — in-process, for tests

There is no [[pipeline.systems]] and no [[pipeline.components]]. Nothing in the service can build a System from a type name, so the keys that once looked as though they could are now parse errors rather than sections that quietly disappear. The same is true of watch, which was documented as hot reload and never implemented. Sources and sinks are the entire factory surface; the pipeline itself arrives either as [pipeline.wasm] or as a Box<dyn PipelineRuntime> handed to ServiceBuilder::with_runtime().

What it refuses to start on

Four checks, in a fixed order, each one a refusal rather than a warning. The order is chosen so that the cheap checks run first: nothing about your component is touched until gate 2.

state already on disk config and host checks the WebAssembly boundary

Checking a config before you deploy

validate runs gates 1 to 3 and exits. It compiles the component and calls describe(), so it catches a stale target_component without moving any data.

Bashand its output
pcs-service validate --config service.toml

OK: all IO targets covered by runtime declared components
OK: config is structurally valid
  node.id:  1
  node.name: pcs-1
  mode:     standalone
  pipeline: pipelines/orders.wasm
  sources:  1
  sinks:    1
  http.bind: 0.0.0.0:8080
  log_level: info
OK: all declared types resolved in built-in registry

A type that no registered factory claims is a warning by default, and the command still exits 0. That is deliberate: a config aimed at a custom binary names factories the stock binary has never heard of. Pass --strict to turn those warnings into a non-zero exit.

File-backed sinks create their output file when the factory runs, which includes running under validate. The parent directory has to exist first.

CommandWhat it does
serve --config f.toml Start. --node-id N overrides node.id; --port P overrides the port in http.bind, and --port 0 prints the OS-assigned address on stdout.
validate --config f.toml Gates 1 to 3, then exit. --strict promotes unknown factory types to errors.
status --addr URL One summary line from /status. --full prints the whole JSON document.
cluster init --config f.toml Pre-flight only: confirms mode = "cluster" and bootstrap = true, then tells you to run serve. It does not start the node.
cluster status --addr URL The cluster field of /status.
cluster join --leader URL
cluster leave		 Not wired to the control plane yet. Both print the manual procedure — edit [[peers]] on every node and restart — and exit 0.

--config and --addr are global, and read PCS_CONFIG / PCS_ADDR from the environment. --log-level and --log-format override [observability].

The HTTP control plane

Four routes on one axum router, bound to http.bind, behind a 10-second request timeout. The server is its own tokio task, and so is the watchdog, so a batch in flight does not stop any of them answering.

the data plane and what it publishes the control plane
EndpointBodyStatus
GET /health { status, uptime_seconds, liveness_counter } 200 while the watchdog counter is within 5 s of uptime; 503 once it falls behind.
GET /ready { status } — ready or not_ready 200 or 503, from one AtomicBool.
GET /metrics Prometheus exposition, version 0.0.4 Always 200. Fed by the OpenTelemetry Prometheus exporter.
GET /status node_id, node_name, mode, uptime_seconds, build.version, plus standalone or cluster Always 200. The block that does not match the mode is null.

In standalone mode the standalone block carries iterations, rows_processed, source_batches_drained, sink_batches_written and iteration_errors. Two honest caveats about the current build: ready is flipped as soon as the runner is spawned rather than after the first successful iteration, and no ClusterProbe is wired into serve yet, so "cluster" reports null even when the node is clustered. /metrics is where the Raft gauges live in the meantime.

Bashwhat a probe pair looks like in practice
curl -sf http://localhost:8080/ready   || echo "not taking work yet"
curl -s  http://localhost:8080/status  | jq '.standalone.iteration_errors'
curl -s  http://localhost:8080/metrics | grep '^pcs_rows_processed_total'

The standard metric names are pcs_pipeline_runs_total, pcs_pipeline_errors_total, pcs_stage_duration_seconds, pcs_source_batches_drained_total, pcs_sink_batches_written_total, pcs_rows_processed_total, pcs_liveness_counter, pcs_ready, pcs_uptime_seconds, and in cluster mode pcs_raft_term, pcs_raft_commit_index and pcs_raft_leader_id. All are registered at startup, so they appear in /metrics before the first increment.

Your own sources, sinks, and runtime

A type string in the TOML is a key into a registry of factories. To add your own, implement one trait and register it before build(). A factory receives the config sub-table as a toml::Value and returns a boxed Source or Sink.

Rustone trait, two methods
use pcs_service::PcsError;
use pcs_service::io::sink::Sink;
use pcs_service::service::registry::SinkFactory;

struct PostgresSinkFactory;

impl SinkFactory for PostgresSinkFactory {
    // This is the string the TOML writes as `type = "PostgresSink"`.
    fn type_name(&self) -> &'static str { "PostgresSink" }

    fn build(&self, config: &toml::Value) -> Result<Box<dyn Sink>, PcsError> {
        let url = config
            .get("url")
            .and_then(toml::Value::as_str)
            .ok_or_else(|| PcsError::configuration("PostgresSink needs a 'url'"))?;
        Ok(Box::new(PostgresSink::connect(url)?))
    }
}

Then assemble the service yourself. register_builtin_factories adds the eight built-ins; your own registrations chain on. Registering the same type_name twice replaces the earlier factory.

Rusta custom binary, WASM pipeline
use pcs_service::service::config::ServiceConfig;
use pcs_service::service::factories::register_builtin_factories;
use pcs_service::service::{ServiceBuilder, run_standalone};
use tokio_util::sync::CancellationToken;

let config = ServiceConfig::load("service.toml")?;

let built = register_builtin_factories(ServiceBuilder::new())
    .register_source(KafkaSourceFactory)
    .register_sink(PostgresSinkFactory)
    .build(&config)?;

// Gate 3 is yours to call: `build()` does not run it.
pcs_service::service::validate_io_coverage(&built.runtime.declared_components(), &config)?;

// `None` opts out of publishing live stats to /status.
let stats = run_standalone(built, &config, CancellationToken::new(), None).await?;

If the pipeline is native Rust rather than a component, hand the builder a runtime directly and leave the [pipeline] table out of the TOML entirely. Any Box<dyn PipelineRuntime> works, and a Pipeline is one.

Rusta native pipeline, no [pipeline] table
let built = ServiceBuilder::new()
    .with_runtime(Box::new(my_pipeline))
    .register_sink(PostgresSinkFactory)
    .build(&config)?;

build() checks pipeline.wasm first. If the config declares a module, that module wins and the runtime you passed to with_runtime is dropped unused. With neither, build() returns a configuration error naming both options.
